name: Enzyme-Substrate Models
what: Two models describe how a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site: the lock-and-key model, where the fit is rigid and pre-formed, and the induced-fit model, where the active site adjusts its shape upon substrate binding.
why: These models explain enzyme specificity at a molecular level and help predict how changes to enzyme structure will affect function.

items.title: I can describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme function
items.what: In the lock-and-key model, the substrate has a shape that is a perfect, rigid fit for the active site of the enzyme before binding occurs — like a specific key fitting a specific lock.
items.why: This model explains why each enzyme is highly specific to its substrate and why molecules with different shapes cannot bind.
items.example: If enzyme X has a triangular active site, only a substrate with a complementary triangular shape will bind. A square-shaped molecule will not fit and cannot be catalysed by enzyme X.

items.title: I can describe the induced-fit model of enzyme function
items.what: In the induced-fit model, the active site is not a perfect fit for the substrate initially. When the substrate binds, the enzyme changes its shape slightly to mould around the substrate, improving the fit.
items.why: The induced-fit model is considered more accurate for many enzymes and better explains how some enzymes can accommodate substrates with slightly varying structures.
items.example: Hexokinase, which catalyses the first step of glycolysis, undergoes a conformational change when glucose binds — the enzyme wraps around the glucose molecule rather than having a pre-formed perfect fit.

items.title: I can compare the lock-and-key and induced-fit models
items.what: Both models agree that the active site and substrate have complementary shapes and charges, and that binding leads to a reaction. They differ in whether the active site shape is fixed (lock-and-key) or flexible (induced-fit).
items.why: Being able to compare the two models is a common exam requirement and demonstrates a deeper understanding of enzyme-substrate interactions beyond a single simplistic description.
items.example: Lock-and-key: the active site shape is set before the substrate arrives. Induced-fit: the active site begins complementary but finishes as a tighter fit after the substrate binds and the enzyme adjusts.
